summary.note: 4-choice random baseline = 25%. Lower solver accuracy = harder.

judge.decisive_mechanism: D pairs a well-tuned adaptive optimizer (Adam, lr=1e-3, wd=0) with a moderate-capacity net (depth-4, width-64) that is the sweet spot for this task: deep enough to compose the multi-term target (cos/sin products, tanh, cubic) yet small enough not to overfit 256 noisy training points. B uses the same good optimizer but is only depth-1/width-128 — it lacks compositional depth and underfits the true signal, so its test MSE is worse. C (depth-6/width-256, RMSprop lr=3e-3, L1) has the most capacity and the most aggressive/unstable optimizer, so it overfits the label noise and/or trains unstably. A (SGD lr=3e-4) is badly undertrained in 2560 steps. So the ordering is A undertrained, C overfit/unstable, B underfit-by-depth, D optimally balanced — D wins on test (noiseless) MSE by best recovering the true function.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Pick the smallest/shallowest net to resist the label noise (std=0.2) — this lands on B, which is what both blind experts chose, and it is WRONG: B is depth-1 and underfits the true multi-term signal. D (depth-4, width-64) is still small enough to resist the noise while being expressive enough to fit the target. The "pick biggest net" (C) and "pick most-regularized/L1" (C) shortcuts also fail. "Pick Adam" does not discriminate because both B and D use Adam at lr=1e-3.

judge.decisive_mechanism: Convergence-within-budget driven by the optimizer/learning-rate pairing, not capacity. A (6-layer, SGD lr=3e-4, no momentum) is badly under-optimized in 2560 steps and is clearly worst. D (Adam lr=1e-2, width-16) is over-aggressive and underpowered. The real contest is B vs C, which are the SAME small residual+LayerNorm+gelu MLP family: B uses Adam lr=3e-3 and reaches a good basin within the 2560-step budget, while C uses AdamW lr=3e-4 (10x smaller LR) and underfits the smooth target in the same budget despite its larger width. Light L1 regularization in B further protects against the std=0.2 training-label noise. So the winner is set by 'fastest well-conditioned optimizer that still generalizes under noise given the budget.'
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Yes. 'Pick the safest-looking regularized / wider net with AdamW + weight decay' selects C, which is WRONG (one blind expert did exactly this). C's 10x-lower LR (3e-4 vs B's 3e-3) makes it underfit within the fixed 2560-step budget. Also 'pick the biggest net' (A, 6 layers) fails hard because SGD at lr=3e-4 barely trains it.

judge.decisive_mechanism: Architecture is identical across all four choices, so it is purely an optimizer race under a short 640-step budget (~160 epochs on 256 points). The winner is the optimizer that combines an adaptive, well-conditioned update (Adam-family, made safe by LayerNorm+residual) with a learning rate high enough to actually converge within the budget: AdamW at lr=3e-3 (B). The other three all underfit for distinct reasons: A is AdamW but at lr=1e-4, far too low to converge in 640 steps; C and D use Adagrad, whose monotonic accumulation of squared gradients decays the effective per-parameter step over training, stalling before convergence (D worse than C due to lower base LR 3e-3 plus weight decay). Overfitting to the train-label noise is not the binding constraint here — underfitting is — so the aggressive, unregularized, adaptive B recovers the noiseless true function best.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Pick the most-regularized config (nonzero weight decay) expecting it to resist the train-label noise: this selects A (AdamW wd=1e-4) or D (Adagrad wd=1e-4), both WRONG, because the regime is underfitting-limited, not overfitting-limited, so weight decay only slows an already-too-slow optimizer. A plain 'pick Adam' heuristic also fails to disambiguate and could land on the low-LR AdamW choice A.
judge.critique: Strong optimizer-only question with a genuine anti-shortcut twist; determinable by mechanics but somewhat textbook, so 4/5.

judge.decisive_mechanism: Optimizer-only comparison (identical architecture/loss/budget across A-D). Under a tight 640-step budget on a LayerNorm + residual MLP, Adam's per-parameter adaptive preconditioning plus momentum (D) converges fastest and best recovers the noiseless test signal. Plain SGD without momentum (B at lr=0.01, C at lr=0.003) converges too slowly in 640 steps — C is worst since its lower lr means even less progress. Adagrad (A) makes early progress but its monotonically accumulating denominator decays the effective step size and stalls late convergence. So the win is driven by convergence speed/conditioning under a short budget, not capacity or regularization.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: "Pick the highest learning rate for fastest convergence in few steps" selects A or B (lr=0.01) over D (lr=0.001) and gives the WRONG answer — it ignores that Adam's adaptive step scaling matters more than nominal lr. ("Pick most regularized" coincidentally lands on D via the 1e-5 weight decay, but for the wrong reason and cannot discriminate A/B/C.)

judge.decisive_mechanism: All four choices share identical architecture and MSE loss; only optimizer+LR vary, so this is purely an optimization/generalization contest under label-noise (train std=0.2, clean test). B (Adagrad lr=0.001) badly underfits — Adagrad's shrinking effective step from an already-tiny base barely moves from init in 640 steps. D (SGD lr=0.003) also underfits: too slow to reach the signal within ~160 epochs. The real contest is C (SGD lr=0.01) vs A (Adagrad lr=0.1). C wins because plain, non-adaptive SGD at a moderate, stable LR generalizes better under label noise (implicit regularization; cf. the marginal-value-of-adaptive-methods result), recovering the true clean-test function, whereas Adagrad's per-coordinate scaling plus an aggressive lr=0.1 fits the noisy training targets more sharply and lands in a worse-generalizing basin. C sits at the 'large-enough-to-learn but stable-and-noise-robust' sweet spot.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Prefer the adaptive optimizer / fastest-progress-in-a-short-budget / most-regularized choice — all point to A (Adagrad lr=0.1, plus weight decay), which is the WRONG answer and exactly where 2/3 experts landed. 'Most regularized' (weight decay present) also favors A/B; the winner C has zero weight decay.

judge.decisive_mechanism: Under deliberately weak optimization (plain SGD, lr=1e-3, no momentum, only 5120 steps), no net reaches its asymptotic capacity, so the winner is decided by early-training conditioning and effective per-step signal, not by expressiveness. Width-256 nets (A, B) get far more useful gradient signal per step than the width-64 nets (C, D), eliminating C and D despite D being the deepest/most-expressive. Between the two wide nets, the decisive axis is residual on/off: B has residual=False, A has residual=True. In a shallow (2-block) wide MLP regressing a noisy 256-point target, the untrained identity/residual paths in A inject raw input and preserve initialization variance, biasing and slowing the fit, while B's plain feed-forward stack with LayerNorm on the output block conditions better and fits the true (noiseless-test) signal faster. Hence B has the lowest mean test MSE over 10 seeds.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Multiple naive heuristics all point away from B: (1) "pick the deepest/most-expressive net for a complex 8D symbolic function" -> D; (2) "pick residual + LayerNorm as the best-regularized/most-modern architecture" -> A (or D); (3) "prefer residual connections, they always help" -> A/C/D, never B. B is the ONLY choice with residual=False, so every 'residual is good' intuition fails. The blind experts picked [D, A, A] -- exactly the deepest and the residual+norm traps -- 0/3 correct.
judge.critique: Strong adversarial item. It cleanly punishes the three dominant shortcuts (biggest/deepest, most-regularized, residual-is-free) and the expert answers [D,A,A] land squarely on those traps, confirming discriminative power. The genuinely testable, robust piece of reasoning is real: weak fixed SGD + short budget makes early-training conditioning and width the driver, killing the narrow C/D even though D looks most expressive -- that alone separates good from shortcut reasoning. The weakness is the final A-vs-B discrimination: both are width-256 with one LayerNorm, differing essentially in residual on/off plus activation/LN placement. The claim that residual HURTS a shallow wide regressor here is directionally defensible but fragile -- its sign depends on init variance, the specific 256-point noisy fit, and 10-seed means, and is not cleanly derivable from first principles the way the width argument is. So a top solver can reliably get to {A,B} but the last bit is closer to a well-motivated guess than a deduction, which is why even the 'wide' reasoners (who chose A) still missed. That fragility caps it below a 5; a cleaner version would make the A/B gap rest on a more robust mechanism. Not indeterminable, though: the correct answer is a plausible-to-strong reasoning target, not noise, so 'partly'.

judge.decisive_mechanism: A is the Goldilocks configuration on the trainability-expressivity-regularization axes. Its residual connections give it usable depth (5x64) to represent the composed trig+cubic+tanh 5D target, while a moderate Adam LR (3e-4) and only light regularization (wd 1e-4, L1 1e-3) let it fit the true signal without overfitting the 256 noisy (std=0.2) training points to the noiseless test set. Every rival fails on exactly one lever: B is too shallow (single hidden layer underfits the structure) and its aggressive lr=1e-3 overfits noise; C is over-regularized and undertrained (tiny lr=1e-4 + heavy L1=0.01 in a short 2560-step budget) so it underfits; D is deep (6 layers, 128) but plain/non-residual, so it is poorly conditioned under a small RMSprop lr=1e-4 and carries no regularization against label noise. A uniquely balances all three.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Pick the biggest/deepest net (D, 6x128) or the most-regularized net (C, L1=0.01 + high wd) or simply the widest (B/D, 128). All three of these surface heuristics point away from the correct A. 'Pick Adam' also fails to disambiguate since both A and B use Adam and B is a trap.
judge.critique: Strong item. The winner is determinable by genuine learning-mechanics reasoning and every naive shortcut (biggest/deepest/widest/most-regularized) misleads, so it tests real intuition about residual connections enabling trainable depth, LR-vs-budget calibration, and regularization-vs-label-noise tradeoffs simultaneously. Both blind experts got A (2/2), consistent with a determinable-but-nontrivial question. Weaknesses keeping it from a 5: (1) the four choices vary model, optimizer, AND loss all at once (mixed axis), so the reasoning is somewhat overdetermined — A wins on multiple independent margins rather than one clean isolated mechanism, which makes it easier to guess for the wrong reasons; (2) the A-vs-C distinction (why heavy L1 + tiny LR underfits rather than helps against noise) is the only genuinely subtle call and depends on the short-budget interaction, which a solver could plausibly miscall while still landing on A; (3) with label noise std=0.2 on only 256 points, seed-to-seed variance could be large, so the 10-seed mean gap between A and the next-best (likely C) should be checked for significance — the prompt's fairness is fine but the margin's robustness isn't visible here.

judge.decisive_mechanism: A pairs a well-conditioned, well-tuned optimizer (AdamW lr=3e-4) with moderate capacity and only light L1 regularization, giving the best bias-variance balance under label-noisy training / noiseless test. Each rival has a disqualifying flaw: B and C use Adagrad, whose monotonically accumulating gradient denominator shrinks the effective step over 2560 steps and underfits (C compounds this with the lowest LR and an over-strong L1 λ=1e-3 on a deep 5-layer net); D uses aggressive RMSprop lr=3e-3 with zero regularization, which chases the std=0.2 label noise and overfits/destabilizes, raising noiseless test MSE. The winner is set by optimizer conditioning + regularization-vs-noise balance, not raw capacity.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: "Pick the biggest/deepest net" selects C (5 layers) or D (width 256), and "pick the most-regularized" selects C (L1 λ=1e-3, 10x A's) — both give the WRONG answer. (Note: the 'pick Adam-family' heuristic does coincidentally land on the correct A.)
judge.critique: Solid multi-axis question: depth, width, optimizer, LR, and loss/regularization all vary, and the train-noise/noiseless-test framing genuinely rewards overfitting-vs-underfitting intuition. The 'biggest net' and 'most-regularized' shortcuts both fail (good discrimination against capacity chasers). Weaknesses: (1) the naive 'prefer Adam' bias happens to land on A, so a shallow optimizer preference is rewarded; (2) A is also moderate/light on essentially every axis, so a cheap 'avoid extremes' heuristic also picks it, partly diluting the deeper mechanism; (3) the real crux A-vs-D hinges on quantitative LR-appropriateness (3e-4 AdamW good vs 3e-3 RMSprop aggressive) that is hard to be certain of from prose. 3/3 blind experts correct with no metrics indicates it is on the easier end of 'deep intuition' but still requires eliminating the Adagrad-underfit and heavy-regularization red herrings.

judge.decisive_mechanism: All choices share the same heavily under-trained optimizer (plain SGD, lr=1e-3, no momentum, only 5120 steps), so asymptotic capacity is NOT the binding constraint — convergence speed and gradient conditioning within a tiny budget are. B (depth 2, width 128, leaky_relu, LayerNorm on both blocks, residual) is the sweet spot: enough width/fan-in to learn the 8-input additive target's features quickly, a short credit-assignment path (depth 2) so gradients propagate cleanly and it converges fastest under slow SGD, non-saturating leaky_relu (no silu flat-region early-learning slowdown), and full normalization stabilizing the effective step size. It beats the wide-shallow extreme A (only one nonlinear stage + slow-to-move 256x256 block + saturating silu) and the narrow-deep extreme D (width 32 underfits, depth 5 converges slowest), plus the less-normalized deeper C.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Pick the biggest / highest-capacity net (Choice A: width 256, ~68k params) because the symbolic target looks rich and noisy — this is the intuitive capacity-driven pick and it is WRONG; it is exactly what all 3 experts chose. The 'most-regularized/smallest to resist label noise' shortcut also fails (points to D). Under slow under-converged SGD, convergence speed beats capacity.
judge.critique: Strong discriminator question. It cleanly separates naive capacity/regularization reasoning from the correct convergence-limited reasoning: the fixed slow plain-SGD budget (lr=1e-3, no momentum, 5120 steps) makes optimization the binding constraint, and the capacity shortcut (pick the widest net A) is a compelling trap that caught all 3 experts. That 0/3 blind experts picked the shortcut answer is good evidence the question rewards deep learning-mechanics intuition rather than surface heuristics. Weaknesses: (1) the winner is only 'partly' determinable — the correct direction (mid-capacity beats the narrow-deep underfit extreme, capacity is not decisive) is derivable, but pinning B specifically over A vs C rests on second-order effects (leaky_relu vs silu early-convergence, one vs two nonlinear stages, LN placement) that honest reasoning can't reliably resolve without running it, so some of the answer is luck. (2) With 4 close-in-capacity residual+LN MLPs under identical hyperparameters, the mean-test-MSE gap between B, A, and C over 10 seeds may be modest, raising a mild significance concern — the margin likely hinges on convergence-rate differences that are real but not large. Overall a good intuition test, slightly limited by the A/B call being closer than a clean mechanistic argument can fully justify.

judge.decisive_mechanism: Under a weak optimizer (plain SGD, lr=3e-4, no momentum, only 5120 steps), all models are in an optimization-limited/underfitting regime (test MSE 0.7-1.1), so the winner is the architecture that optimizes fastest AND has enough capacity to recover a genuinely complex multi-frequency target. C (depth-5, width-128, residual, smooth gelu/silu) wins because residual connections give good gradient flow under weak SGD, and among the residual nets it has the most usable width/capacity (128 > D's 64 > B's 32). A loses decisively (1.10, worst) because it has NO residual connections and only depth 1 — poor conditioning and weak compositional capacity — so its width-256 is wasted. Because it's underfitting-limited, the usual 'noise favors small/regularized model' logic is inverted: more capacity helps.
judge.shortcut_that_fails: Pick the widest / biggest network (A, width 256) as most expressive, or pick the 'simplest, least overfitting-prone' shallow net under label noise — both point to A, which is actually the WORST (test MSE 1.10 vs C's 0.72). A fails because it lacks residual connections and depth, and the regime is optimization-limited underfitting, not overfitting. All 3 experts fell for this (picked A).
judge.critique: Strong discriminative item. It punishes two seductive shortcuts at once (widest-net-wins and simplest-net-generalizes-under-noise), both of which land on the actual worst choice A, explaining the 0/3 expert failure. The decisive lever — residual connections + capacity under a deliberately weak/slow SGD budget, in an underfitting rather than overfitting regime — is a genuine deep-learning-mechanics insight, and the label-noise framing is a red herring that a naive solver over-weights. GT is clean: monotonic ordering matching the mechanism, gap 0.117, win_rate 1.0, C also has the tightest variance. Docked one point because the full ranking within the residual nets (C > B > D, i.e. why width-128 beats width-32 AND width-64 but the target is complex enough that bigger is better) is closer to plausible reasoning than to forced deduction — a careful solver who correctly eliminates A could still split between B/C/D. But eliminating A and identifying 'residual + capacity in an underfit regime' is solidly determinable, so this is a good, not merely lucky, test of intuition.
